summary: Case study converting the two-electron-integral core of GAMESS (12 files, 56,448 lines, 225 subroutines) from fixed-form Fortran 77 to Fortran 2008 with three prompt-specialized Claude Code roles (conversion, testing, review) in separate git worktrees. They work under an agent-authored, version-controlled specification (CLAUDE.md, STYLE_GUIDE.md, AGENT_GUIDE.md) that prescribes a fixed per-file loop, with humans holding shell-approval, adjudication and merge gates. Every file reproduces the 51-test battery bit-for-bit against F77 goldens (612 runs) and passes the maintainers' tolerance-based Jenkins suite. One escaped defect class (a 6-line REAL-to-INTEGER retyping of a packed-label array) was missed by agent-written unit tests and caught by the standard tests; a common-mode blind spot in self-captured goldens was found only by a human-driven build standardization. There is no baseline, cost or human-effort measurement.

claims.claim: All twelve modernized files reproduce the 49 standard GAMESS tests plus two added calculations bit-for-bit (zero chemistry-relevant differences across 612 runs), pass the Jenkins CI suite, and the union build of all 12 also passes
claims.evidence: Table II and §IV-B. The oracle is exact and externally anchored: goldens come from the F77 production build, and Jenkins compares against the expected values GAMESS ships. Limits stated in §V-C: desktop workstation only, extended test suites not run, not integrated into production GAMESS.

claims.claim: A supervised agentic workflow can carry out legacy scientific-code modernization 'at production scale'
claims.evidence: Scope is 12 files, about 5% of a package that 'exceeds a million lines', converted one file at a time with COMMON-block migration explicitly deferred. Nothing is merged to production, and the extended suites and HPC runs are pending (§V-C).

claims.claim: Human effort did not scale with code volume; it concentrated at configuration reconciliation, adjudication and merge decisions
claims.evidence: No human hours, review time or intervention counts are reported. The only timing is the 7 h 29 min sequential validation sweep (about 37 min/file, dominated by the 25-minute standard tests). Who drove each role, which governs the independence the role split is meant to provide (§III-A2), is not stated.

claims.claim: Competence lives in the specification, not the model: work spanned Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7 and Opus 4.8 with no rework when the model changed
claims.evidence: Author testimony only. No mapping of files to models, no per-model success rates, no other model family or runtime; the authors themselves call cross-family portability a conjecture.

claims.claim: Defects that survive a strict compiler are few, tightly clustered and semantically deep; 6 wrong lines out of 55,916, found immediately by running the standard tests
claims.evidence: One escaped defect class: IX retyped REAL(real64) instead of INTEGER(int64), caught on exam01, localized by an agent-written bisection harness over 38 subroutines in five rounds, then generalized into a STYLE_GUIDE audit clause that found two more instances. 11/12 files were arithmetically correct and 11/12 compiled cleanly on first attempt. Authors caution that one project cannot establish an error rate.

claims.claim: Differential checks are blind along their common mode: goldens regenerated alongside the artifact under test cannot catch errors in the procedure that builds both sides
claims.evidence: Three unit-test drivers captured before -fdefault-integer-8 was standardized passed while wrong (26, 36 and 105 changed line pairs once regenerated). The issue was surfaced by a later build standardization, not by any check. Three defects were also found in the oracle tooling itself (timing regex, csh argument parsing, input staging). A concrete mechanism, observed once.

claims.claim: The agentic contribution lies in the 'comprehension minority' (IMPLICIT NONE type inference, INTENT, irreducible GO TO retention, cross-file USE placement) where rule-based transformers fail
claims.evidence: Argued from examples (718 annotated retained GO TOs, circular-dependency avoidance in the eftei family). The authors concede plusFORT/SPAG handle a 'substantial share' of the edits and were not run (§II-B), and that a rule-based tool would have made the same IX mistake. There is no measured comparison.

patterns.note: The specification prescribes a fixed per-file sequence: branch, read original, write .f90 + change log + unit-test driver, compile dependencies in a fixed order, capture the F77 golden, compile under -std=f2008 and diff, build the full binary and run 51 standard + Jenkins tests, then human review. Each file must produce a four-artifact contract. The authors say outright that 'the per-file loop is prescribed by the specification rather than planned per file'. There is no comparison with an unprescribed Claude Code loop or with a rule-based tool.

No LLM-generated task DAG. File order and dependency compilation order are fixed by humans and the build; agents plan only within a file (which constructs to restructure, how to sequence declaration inference).

Exact, externally anchored execution oracle gates every merge and caught the one escaped defect. Agent-written synthetic unit tests (about 255,000 quartets) missed it because the faulty path only fires under sustained enumeration, and self-captured goldens had a common-mode blind spot. The verifier helps only to the extent that at least one layer is anchored to a reference not regenerated alongside the artifact.

Three agent-authored, human-approved specification files govern the work; one audit rule was added by an agent after diagnosing its own defect and retroactively found two more instances. No comparison with an unspecified or human-written specification.
CLAUDE.md auto-loaded every session, pointing to the other two documents; an agent trimmed it from 243 to 176 lines to save context. Host-specific (Claude Code convention).

Strict -std=f2008 compilation caught interface and literal-form defects cheaply, and the review role runs grep-style style checks (Table I), including a COMMON-count check that makes silently skipped deferrals mechanically detectable.

Humans approve side-effecting shell commands, reconcile build configuration, adjudicate results and give two approvals per merge plus CI. The common-mode blind spot was found by human-driven cross-checking. No measurement of gate load or of what the gates caught beyond that anecdote.

Three roles are prompt specializations of one tool, explicitly 'not a multi-agent system in the coordination sense'. Their value is independent checking, which the paper notes is weakened if one operator drives all three; who drove them is not reported.
Each role uses its own git worktree and they coordinate only through the shared repository. Isolation is for independence, not parallel throughput; the validation sweep ran sequentially.

Concedes that rule-based restructuring tools (plusFORT/SPAG) already cover the mechanical majority of edits, but none was run, so the split between deterministic and agent work is asserted rather than measured.

methodology.sample: One codebase: 12 GAMESS source files (8 int2 + 4 eftei), 56,448 F77 lines, 225 subroutines; 51-test battery x 12 files = 612 runs, plus Jenkins (49 tests per file) and a union build.
methodology.baselines: None. No rule-based converter, no human conversion, and no differently structured agent setup.
methodology.models: Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7 and Opus 4.8; no other runtime or model family.
methodology.variance: Not applicable to the bit-exact verdicts; no repeated conversions of the same file to measure run-to-run variation.
methodology.ablations: None. The specification, role split and human gates are never removed or varied.
methodology.contamination_controls: Not discussed. GAMESS source is downloadable, but correctness is judged by exact reproduction of physical outputs, so memorization cannot inflate the verdict.

standards.artifacts: Two GitHub repositories (gms-bbg/test-validation; shenyuzhong/gamess-modernization-paper). The modernized GAMESS source cannot be shipped because of licensing; whether the specification files and prompts are included is not stated in the paper.

biases.detail: One codebase, 12 files, one escaped defect class; error-profile conclusions rest on n=1.
Only Anthropic models and the Claude Code runtime; model portability is asserted within one vendor family.
Agents wrote the unit tests and captured the goldens they were checked against. The authors include the GAMESS maintainers, so the team evaluating the workflow also adjudicates acceptance.
No token, dollar or human-hour figures, so the claim that human effort did not scale with code volume cannot be checked.
Rule-based tools the paper says cover most edits were not run, and no human or unprescribed-agent conversion is compared.
'Production scale' for an unmerged 12-file subset of a million-line package; 'difficult to describe as anything but agentic work' for an agent trimming its context file.

verdict_reason: The bit-exact outcome on a hard, real codebase is credible because the oracle is exact and anchored outside the agents, and the defect and common-mode analysis is careful and useful. But it is a single uncontrolled case study: no baseline (including the rule-based tools the paper concedes do most of the edits), no cost or human-effort data behind the 'effort did not scale' claim, anecdotal model portability, and an unmerged 12-file subset described as production scale.
applicability: For the team's DAG question, this is evidence that a fixed per-unit loop written into the specification (read, transform, compile strictly, check against a golden, integrate, human merge), driven by an ordinary agent host, was enough for a large mechanical-plus-judgement migration. No LLM-generated DAG was needed: unit order and dependency compile order were fixed by humans and the build, and cross-file reasoning happened inside the loop. It is not evidence that the fixed loop beat an unconstrained agent. The transferable parts for a Java team running something like a Spring Boot or jakarta migration across four repos are: (1) a per-module artifact contract (change, change log, test, golden); (2) strict compiler and linter settings as a cheap first gate; (3) at least one oracle anchored to outputs captured once from the old production build, such as recorded ingestion outputs or contract tests, never regenerated alongside the change; (4) mechanical counts (for example every deferred item annotated) so skipped work is detectable; (5) deterministic recipes (OpenRewrite) for the mechanical majority, which this paper concedes but did not test. The specification here is CLAUDE.md-bound; for mixed hosts the same contract belongs in a portable AGENTS.md plus CI checks. It transfers only where an exact or strong reference oracle exists, which healthcare-education content ingestion can approximate with golden snapshots.

conflicts_with.detail: AgentModernize's structured multi-agent modernization pipeline reaches about 23% behavioural equivalence and loses to a single prompt for stronger models. Here a spec-prescribed per-file loop with frontier models reaches 100% bit-exact equivalence. The two differ in language pair (cross-language COBOL/PL-SQL to Python vs in-language F77 to F2008), in models, and in the oracle, which is exact and externally anchored here.
